spec.cue: A soft, nearly colourless picture, with sound and touch doing much of the seeing.

cpd.note: measured values run from 1.6 in a manatee to 11.5 in a harbour seal under water; the pick of 4 lies between a humpback whale and a Bryde's whale and is the app's

fov.note: the middle of the 120 to 130 degrees given for a bottlenose dolphin; using it for seals and whales too is the app's choice

M.note: one kind of cone and no blue-sensitive cone; the single-sensor mapping is the app's reading

gain.note: worked out from a dolphin seeing 0.5 log units better than a person in dim light

sheen.note: many cetaceans and seals have a reflecting layer behind the retina; how strong the sheen looks is the app's choice

CONE_L.note: one long-wavelength cone pigment, as found in whales and seals studied

k.note: how strongly sounds heard by the microphone ring across the picture

rows: Retinal sharpness runs from about 1.6 cycles per degree in a manatee to 3.3 in a humpback whale and 4.8 in a Bryde's whale. A harbour seal reaches 11.5 under water. Yours is many times higher. We blur the picture to about 4.

Whales and seals that have been studied carry only one kind of cone, the long-wavelength kind, and lack the blue-sensitive kind, so they are essentially colour-blind. A dolphin's cone pigment peaks near 522 to 524 nanometres. We draw the picture with that single colour sensor. Manatees are the exception, with two kinds of cone.

Rorquals, right whales and sperm whales have lost the genes for both cone pigments, so their vision rests on rods alone. The rod pigment of a grey whale peaks at 492 nanometres and that of an elephant seal near 483, in the blue-green.

A bottlenose dolphin's two eyes together cover about 120 to 130 degrees, and the two views overlap in only 20 to 30 degrees. A sperm whale has the same panoramic field with no overlap. We squeeze the picture to 125 degrees.

A bottlenose dolphin sees 0.5 log units better than a person in dim light, which is about three times more light, and 0.2 log units worse in bright light. Many cetaceans and seals have a reflecting layer behind the retina, while manatees lack one. We brighten the picture about three times and add a faint sheen.

A bottlenose dolphin sends clicks between 40 and 150 kilohertz and can notice a change in echo delay as small as 1 microsecond. The sonar scene for small objects reaches about 100 metres. With the microphone on, this view can draw sound as rings across the picture.
A harbour seal can follow the wake of a fish for up to 30 seconds after it has passed, using whiskers that respond best between 10 and 100 hertz. No phone senses this, so it is left out.

The pick of 4 for sharpness, the 125 degree field, the single-sensor colour mapping, the threefold brightness gain, the sheen and the strength of the sound rings are the app's. The records cover many species that differ a good deal, so one view stands for all of them.

sound.name: rings
sound.note: sounds heard by the microphone spread as rings across the picture, in the spirit of dolphin clicks

claims.how: 4 lies between the humpback whale value of 3.3 and the Bryde's whale value of 4.8 cycles per degree.
125 is the middle of the 120 to 130 degrees given for the bottlenose dolphin.
The matrix name stands for one cone pigment near 524 nm (R37) with no blue-sensitive cone (R46); turning that into a matrix is the app's mapping.
The pigment peak of 524 nm is the upper end of the 522 to 524 nm range given for dolphin and porpoise long-wavelength pigment.
A dolphin is 0.5 log units more sensitive than a person in dim light, and 10 to the power 0.5 is about 3.16.

quotes.quote: we estimated the peak anatomical spatial resolving power in water to be 4.8 cycles/degree and 3.3 cycles/degree in the Bryde's whale and the humpback whale, respectively
